utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case -- Ms. Registrar. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we please have the appearances for the day, starting with the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Bronagh McKenna, Dan Saxon, and Inger de Ru for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Perisic is represented today by Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Boris Zorko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness that we would like to call is Stojan Malcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness to come in, I would like to say for the benefit of the OTP that Mr. Malcic is in a very bad health state. He has suffered two strokes. And I advised him that whenever he needs to have a break during this trial, he should ask for it, but I hope everything will run smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic, for letting us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you please tell us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Stojan Malcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, two things at the beginning. What I told you during briefing, you see a screen in front of you and you can see that the record is being noted. This will give you a guidance when you should start giving your answer. We both speak the same language and we both speak rather fast.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Secondly, the Trial Chamber has been advised about your health state so whenever you need to take a break during examination, please say so and the Trial Chamber will accommodate you. So please be relaxed.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, I'll go briefly through your CV. Can you tell us first when were you born?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of February, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The village of Rekavica, Banja Luka municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You completed the military and economic academy in 1971; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you completed a high political school of the JNA. Do you remember in what year?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the mid-1980s. I don't remember the exact year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After completing the military academy, you were in various positions in troops up until 1976, and after that you were transferred to the centre of high military schools in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: After I finished the military academy, I was assigned to the garrison of Sarajevo, the centre of military high schools, where I discharged a variety of duties in compliance with my rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You started working on personnel issues in 1984; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1989, you were appointed chief of the organ for organisation and mobilisation changes in this high school centre in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991, in September, you were appointed head of the courses that were being conducted in the centre in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time become a member of a different army?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1992, I became a member of the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were appointed there, as your first post, assistant chief of the department for personnel issues in the administration for organisation and personnel attached to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down and wait for me to finish my question. So far the interpreters are coping but maybe we shall face problems later on. What rank did you hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You held the same rank in the JNA before that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of June, 1993, you were appointed head of the department for personnel in the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel issues in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were given an extraordinary promotion to the rank of colonel on the 16th of December, 1992, in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your professional service terminated and you were retired in Yugoslavia by the competent organ of the VJ on the 31st of August, 1997?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are currently in retirement and you live in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Practically most of your service, while you were in the JNA, you spent in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I spent the whole service with the JNA in the Sarajevo garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, when you became a member of the VRS, can you tell me the location of your service at that time?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From the 30th of May, 1992, I spent the entire service in the VRS with the Main Staff of the VRS discharging the duties relating to the personnel organ in the sector for mobilisation and organisation of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the location?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak. Towards the end of 1996, we moved to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, we shall now move on to our first subject. Since you were stationed in Sarajevo before the outbreak of the conflict, can you tell us briefly what was the atmosphere prevailing in Sarajevo in the spring of 1992? And I'm particularly referring to the months of April and May.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was stationed at the Marshal Tito barracks in Sarajevo. To put it simply, the situation was difficult and horrible. From the 1st of March, 1992, when at Bascarsija a member of a wedding party was killed in front of an Orthodox church, all the Serbs in Sarajevo started fearing for their safety. Panic set in, people were afraid. Then the Serbs started to send their family members outside of the city of Sarajevo for safety reasons. The majority of them were dispatched to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, more precisely to Belgrade. They used all kinds of transportation means; by plane, by train, by buses. That went on like that up until mid-April. After that, armed clashes started breaking out at various locations. Transportation links to Belgrade were severed, both road and railway transportation, and after that, air transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do with your family?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of April 1992, I sent my two daughters to Gacko to my mother-in-law and to my wife's brother because they lived in Gacko. I remained at the Marshall Tito barracks, and I stayed there around the clock with the cadets who were undergoing training there. Those were young men between the ages of 16 and 20. I wanted to be with them, to encourage them, and to prevent them from being afraid and thereby doing some undesirable acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now what happened to you, yourself, in early May? Can you describe this event, please.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of May, 1992, was a nice and sunny day. On the street of Vojvoda Stepa Stepanovic that ran past our barracks was full of people strolling around, civilian people. There was no shooting in the city of Sarajevo on that morning. I had to go to my flat to take some medicines for my younger daughter who suffers from epilepsy and to give the medicines to my wife who was living in our flat at the time. I was given an approval from my superior to go out for about two hours, and I remembered that I went out between the hours of 1200 and 1400 because that was quite sufficient time for me to go to the flat and come back. When I left the barracks and when I headed towards my flat at some 200 or 250 metres from the barracks in front of the secondary school of economics, there was a patrol, a police patrol in blue uniforms. They stopped me and asked for my ID, seemingly accidently because that's what they told me, let us just see your ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, because no one was allowed to walk in uniform around Sarajevo at the time. When the policemen saw that my name was Stojan Malcic in my ID, he started insulting me, calling me a Chetnik, and that he would have to carry out a special task in relation to me. They took me into one of the rooms in the secondary school of economics and handed me over to another policeman. Actually, there were two policemen but in plain clothes. They had rifles, they had belts, they had some knives and some grenades attached to the belt. One of them hit me and then ordered me to lie down on the concrete floor. He hit me again, and this blow made me fall on to the ground. Then the two of them started kicking me, hitting me with rifle-butts, and cursed my Chetnik mother. When they got tired of that, they called by phone someone else to come in. After some ten minutes, another person arrived. It was a superior of his -- of theirs. He ordered me to get into his car, which was a kind of jeep. He drove me in the direction of my flat, and I thought I was going to my flat, in fact; however, he took me to a cellar in one of the four high-rise buildings that were next to the building where my flat was. And across the street was the elementary school called at the time Ivan Goran Kovacic. This is where they beat me even worse, where they treated me badly. They beat me unconscious. At one point when I lost consciousness, they poured some dirty water over my head from a bucket and they allowed me to come to. Then he took out a knife from a shield -- sheath at the belt and that was actually a knife that was a component part of an automatic rifle used by the JNA and it was a very sharp knife, like a razor. He put the knife against my throat and then, on the 6th of May, he told me that I was the eighth in a row of people that he was going to kill by slitting their throats. Then he took a pistol, put it in my mouth, and then he said, It is better yet if I put the pistol in your mouth and blow your head. After that he gave up on the idea. Another person who was an associate of his approached me because I told them that I was a lieutenant-colonel employed at the Marshall Tito barracks to which they responded that their duty was probably to report this to the military police. He made a phone call. I don't know who he called. After this telephone conversation, he told me that he was very sorry for having to make this phone call because he would have been happy to cut my head off and to throw me in the yard of a nearby school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me where were you transferred after that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He called another person by phone, and they ordered them take me to Omar Maslic Street police station. They took me there and left me in a corridor. I stayed there for a short period of time, then military police arrived with a jeep and took me to the TO building or actually the building that belonged to the TO before the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please switch off the microphone while the witness is talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, the interpreters ask that you please switch off your mic when the witness is talking. As a result, they did not finish the witness's answer. Please ask the witness to complete that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that they took you to the TO building, that was something before that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence building, that is what it was at the time. The Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, please, because I'd like us to move on to some other topics now. How long were you locked up there, and what happened after a while? Were you exchanged? Did you leave those premises?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From the TO staff, I was transferred to the central prison that was previously the central prison of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. I was kept there at that prison as a JNA prisoner. There were other officers in that prison too, officers of the JNA who had also been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, we have a correction for the transcript. Was this a JNA prison or was this a prison where JNA members were detained?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian prison of the Ministry of the Interior, whereas we as soldiers were being detained there when that war started, when these problems in Sarajevo started. On the 4th floor, that was the last floor where they put us officers at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among the prisoners, was there anyone from Dobrovojacka Street? I don't want us to go to the incident that occurred on the 3rd of May. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see anyone in that prison; I was in my own cell all day long with two unknown men whom I first met then. They continued torturing us in that prison. The torture was psychological rather than physical. Every evening we were transferred to a different cell, and they were telling us that they would take us out to execute us. It was very hard to survive in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, do you remember the day when you were exchanged and where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 13th of May, 1992, on the separation line at Stupska Petlja on the road towards Ilidza. So that was the metropolitan area of town. There was a separation line already then between the two warring sides, and the two commissions met up there, the exchange commissions. I was exchanged for two officers whom I did not know and who were brought to that separation line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak into microphone, to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, the interpreters ask you to please get closer to the microphone so that they can hear what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it can be a bit more comfortable for you if you pull up your chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just have a correction here. Do you remember how many of you were exchanged on this side, JNA officers, and how many were on the other side, how many persons, roughly; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were four members of the JNA. We were exchanged for six members of the Territorial Defence, if I can call it that way. I mean, at first they were a paramilitary, but that's what they called themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you go from there? And just tell us actually where you went from there, just give me a brief answer.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was taken to the Lukavica garrison clinic so that I would be given medical assistance straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long were you in that clinic in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I was just examined there. They gave me certain therapy. And then I was returned to this building in Lukavica because the clinic, the infirmary, had to deal with patients who were a lot more serious than me, they were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say a different building, is that within the barracks, the complex of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: It's within the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks in Lukavica consisting of several buildings. There was a building where soldiers slept, there was a building where the command was. All that before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago when we were speaking about your CV, you said that you became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 30th of May. Could you please tell us how that happened, how come you were in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From the 13th of May until the 30th of May, and I was exchanged on the 13th of May, I was at the Lukavica barracks because I had to go to the infirmary every day for medical treatment. I was in contact with officers whom I knew and who were also in Lukavica, and from them I heard that the Presidency of the SFRY had made a decision and that was made public on the 5th of May, I think, 1992. It was made public through the media, namely, that the JNA units should withdraw to the territory of the FRY until the 19th of May, 1992, and that officers born in Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain in Bosnia in the Army of Republika Srpska. I think it had a different name then, at the very beginning, but it's that army. That was it as far as I was concerned. I was born in Banja Luka and that meant that I should stay in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Do you know the date when the Army of Republika Srpska was officially established?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Officially, the Army of Republika Srpska was established on the 12th of May, 1992, at the Assembly of Republika Srpska in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go on. What were you told and who was it that said that to you?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The 4th Corps was in the garrison in Sarajevo, JNA corps that is. And it was in Lukavica actually. So I found out from these officers that this decision had been made and that we who would stay on in the Army of Republika Srpska would continue to receive income that amounted to our salaries while we were in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that what you were told while you were still in Lukavica or were you told later?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, while I was still in Lukavica that that decision had been made that those who stayed would continue to receive their salary, so I would receive my salary as if [Realtime transcript read in error "salaries if"] I were still a JNA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how is it that you came to Han Pijesak, who did you report to, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, 1992, an officer came, a signalsman, a colonel whom I knew from earlier on because he was chief of communications in the 2nd Military District. He said, I had such trouble finding you, because he heard from other officers that I had been exchanged and that I was in Lukavica. He said that I was supposed to go to the Main Staff, to the personnel department, that they did not have a single personnel officer there. Also, by way of a joke, he said, Well, that's your orders. And I said, Yes, sir; again, by way of a joke. And I got into the car and went with him to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very sorry to interrupt, just a concern about the transcript before we lose page 13 from our screen. At line 14 of page 13, I heard the English translation: "... so I would receive my salaries as if I were a -- as if I were still a JNA member. But the word "as" does not appear yet in the transcript. I just want --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: What the interpreter said was "my salary," in the singular, "as if I were still a JNA member."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It would be best if I asked the witness. What is it that you said about your salary?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: What I was told was that all of the JNA members who were to stay on in the Army of Republika Srpska would have the right to receive a salary and other income as if they were members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who did you report to in Han Pijesak, and was the Main Staff established by then?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska consisted of a small number of officers then in Han Pijesak. They already knew about the organisational structure of the Main Staff, because at the time they worked on that, however, a final decision hadn't been made yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What was this final decision that hadn't been made yet?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: There was no information printed yet, nothing. There was just a draft, how this was supposed to be. But we thought that things would be the way we decided then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to establish a Main Staff, what has to be done? What kind of book, what kind of form?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't actually give you an answer as to who I reported to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please let's clarify this matter now, but I need it clarified for the transcript, and then you will tell me.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: In order to establish a Main Staff in all units and an organisational structure of the Army of Republika Srpska, it was indispensable to first create an organisational structure, and then, on that basis, to work out the establishment according to regulations that were accessible to us at the time, and those were JNA regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now let us go back to that question. Who was it that you reported to when you came to Han Pijesak and what were you told?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I reported to Colonel Milan Lukic who was chief of the personnel department in the administration for personnel and organisation. He told me that I was his assistant, that we were supposed to establish our department, and for the time being it would be the two of us doing all the work to the best of our ability and within the time we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 16 on page 15, he said that he said to you that you were supposed to form, right?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: That was our priority task.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were your offices?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: At the time, the offices of the Main Staff were in the area of the command of the former JNA, for war-time needs, that is. We were put up where the officers -- or rather, where the soldiers were that provided security for the building. There were quite a few officers there from the command of the 2nd Military District. After what happened in Dobrovojacka Street where they had been taken prisoner and mistreated -- and there were casualties there as well, as you know; both soldiers and officers were killed there. Those who had been born on the territory of the FRY said that they wanted to go to the territory of the FRY, and then they were waiting for transportation so that they would be transferred to the territory of the FRY in an organised fashion. Their families had already been taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it that you decided then? Could you go along with them or not?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Then and in Lukavica I decided that I would remain at the Army of Republika Srpska because I was born in Banja Luka in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that's where my entire family and all my relatives live. And I even sent my children to say within the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I didn't have any close relatives in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you mentioned a few moments ago in Han Pijesak from the former JNA, did the -- did you stay there in those prefabricated buildings, the ones that you referred to, did you stay there throughout your service?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Up until the end of 1992, we were all in Crna Rijeka on those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. What you said a few moments ago, that was the previous command post of the JNA, is that what is called Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did I hear you say at page 16 line 22 that up until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's what the witness said, "up until the end." Yes, you understood it correctly. "Up until the end of 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were there in Crna Rijeka as well, right, in these prefabricated buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So where did you go after that, your sector, your service?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, we just need the witness's answer to be recorded on page 17, line 6. The witness's answer was "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Malcic, the interpreters are already telling us that they did not hear what you said. You will have to pause a bit before starting to answer, and I will do the same. My question was --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Since we established the Main Staff already during 1992, more officers came, so the personnel level of the Main Staff went up. In those premises there simply wasn't enough room for the entire Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you move then?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: A decision was made to establish a rear command post of the Main Staff. And it was decided that it will be in the Gora hotel in Han Pijesak. The logistical sector was moved to this new command post, as well as the sector for organisation and mobilisation, the financial administration, and the sector for information and religious affairs. From December 1992 onwards until December 1996, I was in hotel Gora in Han Pijesak working at my sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how far were Han Pijesak and hotel Gora from Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres by road, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was my question. You said that at the beginning you were appointed assistant chief for personnel affairs. This personnel department was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period, the personnel department was part of, initially, administration for organisation and personnel issues, and from mid-1993, of the sector for organisation and mobilisation issues. And that name remained until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to your department, your sector, do you remember what other departments there were?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: In addition to the personnel department, if I remember correctly, there was a department for organisation and establishment, a section for recruitment and mobilisation, and a information technology organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From your CV we saw that at one point you were appointed chief of the personnel department. Who was the head of the sector that you just mentioned to which your department was subordinated, and during the war were there any changes in personnel terms in this post?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Mr. Lukic. You are asking the question of subordination a second time. The first time you asked for it -- you asked it was at page 18, line 8 to 9. It has never been answered. Secondly, this question that you are now asking has got so many questions that I think you should break it up into pieces. You know, you are saying from your CV, and then who was the head, and then during the war who was subordinated -- to whom was he subordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just see whether an answer was given or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your personnel department was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, to the chief of administration for organisation and personnel. Later, this name was changed to sector for organisation and mobilisation issues, but their remit actually remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that your direct superior was Milan Lukic as the head of the personnel department?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: When I joined --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the answer. There was a slight overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness is requested to please repeat as there was overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your last answer.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, when I joined the General Staff -- actually, the Main Staff of the VRS - there's some confusion between these two terms sometimes - I was assistant chief of the personnel department who at the time was Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question was who he was subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He was subordinated to the head of the administration for organisation and personnel who at the time was Mico Grubor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was Mico Grubor constantly indisposed until the end of the war, or was he replaced by someone?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He was the assistant --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please speak slowly, there are two many titles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking that the witness please speak slowly. There are too many titles that are being mentioned. Can we go back to try and start that answer. "He was the assistant ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, since there's a lot of information, can you tell us what Mr. Mico Grubor's function was?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: We did some re-organisation at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his position on the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From May 1992 until mid-1993, he was chief of administration for organisation and personnel issues. In mid-1993, there were some changes in our establishment so this title was changed. So he became assistant chief of the Main Staff of the VRS in charge of organisation, mobilisation, and personnel issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he replaced at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: That's what you asked me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat everything, just give us clear-cut answers. How long he held this position and who succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Mico Grubor remained in this position until September 1994. He was succeeded by Petar Skrbic, and he remained in that post until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you became head of the personnel department, who was your direct superior?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: When Milan Lukic, due to health reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us be very clear with questions and answers. We don't have to go into the reasons of some -- why something happened.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: When I was head of the personnel department, my direct superior was Mico Grubor, and later on Mr. Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were your initial tasks once you were appointed to this post in the personnel department? What did you have to do at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: When I joined the Main Staff in May or June 1992 along with Milan Lukic, we worked on establishing this personnel department. Then we proceeded with collecting information from lower ranking units of the VRS about which officers of the former JNA remained in Republika Srpska, because the task of our department was to set up records and gather documents for the purpose of regulating the status of officers and civilians who had been in the JNA but now were in the VRS after the 20th of May which was the dead-line for the JNA to withdraw to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who kept records about ordinary troops and about reserve officers of the JNA; did that have anything to do with your department?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't. These records were kept by lower-ranking units for their own purposes, and they did it in compliance with the then-applicable rules and regulations, the ones that we applied at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter document of Defence 00826D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are going to see on your screen a document, Mr. Malcic, and I'm going to ask you what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please first look at page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are both in the B/C/S. Can we have the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 2 or, rather, the last one in both versions. This document consists of four pages altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, are you familiar with this document? Can you tell us in a few words what this is?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: These were the orders of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS to proceed with the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska. As I can see here, an organisational structure of the VRS is already in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was engaged in drafting this order and the organisation?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Those involved in drafting this order was actually the product of a team-work by all the officers from the Main Staff but subject to approval by the corps commanders, not consent. I correct myself, assistance rather than consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to go through some basic structural units. Number one is Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I can't see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to page 1 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So item number 1 on page 1 specifies the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was called at the time, then we have operation groups as follows. I'm going to read them out first. The 1st Krajina Corps, then on the next page we have the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2, please. And in English please as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The corps command was in Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then can we move on to the next page in B/C/S and let's stay on the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see here that the next one is Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, followed by the Eastern Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we have Herzegovina Corps, and then we have branch units and institutions, logistics units, and air force and anti-aircraft defence as a separate organisational unit. First of all, tell me whether these corps as listed here in this document dated the 16th of June, 1992, remained with this same structure until the end of war?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was another corps formed in the meantime, and do you know roughly when?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: To my recollection towards the end of 1992, the Drina Corps was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document to be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D00290, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 290, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have us look at another document now on our screens. It is from the Defence 65 ter list, 00825D. [In English] 825D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Malcic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a bit? I can barely see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Malcic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This is a document that is more detailed than the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In which sense detailed?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Here we have the organisational structure of the Main Staff with the codes that we used from the former JNA for the establishment of such units. Every unit has its own number in peacetime, and in war they have their peacetime location, their mobilisation location, they have their own military post code in peacetime and in war time and also their numbers, their names. We did not invent them; they were already in the code tables on the basis of which information was provided earlier on in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this information that entered your establishment when the establishment of the VRS was made?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This was entered into the establishment information that we printed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see here that the date is the 18th of June, 1992, when this order was made. Do you know roughly how long this work went on in establishment, and once this establishment was completed here in the Main Staff, what was done then?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This was the basic document that made it possible to make it possible to move on to the actual organisation and establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska as spelled out here. We then worked day and night in co-operation with all officers of the Army of Republika Srpska from the Main Staff and from subordinate units who could provide adequate assistance to us. Because the basic objective was to set up establishment as soon as possible and to link up all units into an organisational hole to have a proper system of command from platoon level all the way up to the level of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see at page 24, line 23, you are interpreted as having said the date of this order is the 18th of June, 1992. Is that the date or am I seeing -- looking at something different on my screen? Mine is dated the 16th of June. By a commander of the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina 16th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you look at the numbers in B/C/S, Your Honours, well, the witness knows, perhaps he can say for himself. It's better if he says what date it is rather than have us interpret it. Could we please zoom in on the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can see the date in B/C/S. Thank you so much. So it means the translation is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not quite sure. I'm looking at the document here on my Case Manager's screen, perhaps it is the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this document passed on the same day like the previous one, Mr. Malcic? Maybe you are right, perhaps it is actually the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the date please be enlarged in B/C/S and I'll ask Mr. Malcic too whether he remembers perhaps. Because we know the previous document is the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Now, whether it's the 16th or 18th, it's pretty dark here, so it's either the 16th or the 18th. I think it's the 18th, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's the 18th as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at that figure 18 and the figure that denotes the month, would you say they look alike or don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It certainly happened in June. Now I can see it; it's the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Poor photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can take the break now, or, rather, I'd like to tender it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D00291, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that would be a convenient moment. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska was completed, what did you do then in relation to the personnel affairs that you actually dealt with?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: When the establishment was put in place, I, as personnel officer, immediately started giving specific duties to specific soldiers and officers as their superiors had decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on we are going to analyse the army, the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, but do you perhaps know when this Law on the Army of Republika Srpska was passed?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I think it was the end of June 1992, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, according to the rules of the former JNA, what does the personnel dossier of an active-duty officer or soldier contain?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: There were instructions as to what it should contain. Basic data is entered immediately upon completion of military school, including the grades they had, then their first performance assessment as soon as they start working, and then later every change in terms of their service was entered into the dossier file. There were two actually dossiers, DP 1 and DP 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what they were marked?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: DP 1 and DP 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine, yes, it's there in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Personnel dossier number 1 and personnel dossier number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was whether there was -- the abbreviation was DPP 1 or DPP 2 and the witness said they called it in abbreviated terms.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Personnel dossier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember during the former JNA where were these dossiers kept, DP 1 and DP 2?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: DP 1 was in the personnel administration, and DP 2 was kept with the personnel organ, the officer in charge of regulating a particular person's status in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say personnel administration, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The personnel administration of the JNA, while I worked in the JNA that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, this personal administration where DP 1 was kept or was that within the unit?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The personnel administration was either in the General Staff or the ministry; I cannot remember exactly now. But at any rate, it was at the highest level of control and command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say the officer in charge who kept DP 2, can you give us a specific example when you were in the JNA at the centre of higher schools in Sarajevo? Where was your DP 1 and where was your DP 2?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: My DP 1 was at the personnel administration, and the DP 2 was kept by the deputy chief of the General Staff for the KoV --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DP 2 was kept with the deputy chief of the General Staff for KoV where the personnel organ was. That was the organisational organ of the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does KoV stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dossier of personnel information number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the JNA was withdrawn from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in relation to the units that were in the 2nd Military District beforehand, where were these DP 2s, these personnel files, at the moment before withdrawal and where were they after withdrawal?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Before withdrawal, DP 2 for NCOs as far as I can remember -- well, it was the corps commander who regulated the situation for non-commissioned officers, so this DP 2 was kept by the personnel organ at the corps command. For all officers, this DP 2 was at the command of the 2nd Military District as it was known at the time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These parts of personnel dossiers, when the JNA units left Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they stay in Sarajevo or did they accompany the unit as it were?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear on that, what happened to the DP 2s that were kept by the personnel organ of the 2nd Military District. Because on the 2nd of May or, rather, on the 3rd of May, the incident at Dobrovojacka Street happened where many officers and soldiers got killed and the entire documentation and materiel resources that were part of that convoy were destroyed. I do not know about any of that being taken out of Sarajevo before that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not being clear. This documentation, was it supposed to leave the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the JNA withdraw or was it supposed to remain in, say, in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to leave with that unit to the same location where the unit was being sent and then a decision would ultimately be made what would be done with the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, in the personnel department of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, did you make any personnel documentation and personnel dossiers? How did you deal with this personnel information then?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Immediately in June, an order was made on the powers of officers for regulating the status in service. I think that's what the document was called. Every officer in charge would establish his dossier for a professional military soldier. I, in the personnel department, established an original dossier, as I said, for all military officers who were supposed to regulate the status of persons serving for the chief of Main Staff. From lower ranking subordinates, I received certain documents that I used for regulating their status, and I was supposed to look into how this was dealt with in subordinate units. We had our own database in the computer, and this was indispensable for us so that we could regulate the status of each and every professional officer and every civilian serving in the Army of Republika Srpska. Those who stayed on after the JNA withdrew into the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that in June an order was passed about regulating status in service. Whose order was this; of the Army of Yugoslavia or the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska was adopted, bylaws were supposed to be passed and the minister of defence of the Army of Republika Srpska passed that regulation for regulating the status of military officers in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to have a document from our 65 ter list, or, rather, the Prosecution 65 ter list. 9230 is the document I'd like to have. Your Honour, this is the organisational schematic that was used by Mr. Harmon in his opening statement. I am not going to tender it, but I would like the witness to use this schematic in order to deal with certain questions. 65 ter 9230 is what I'd like to have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is in English, Mr. Malcic, but I'm going to ask you questions about particular individuals, certain officers. I would like to know whether the persons I'm going to mention to you now were members of the Army of Republika Srpska from the very outset when it was established and during the course of 1992, so that first period as it were. First I'm going to ask you about General Ratko Mladic, whether he was in the Army of Republika Srpska from the very outset?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the very outset when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, he was in the Army of Republika Srpska, and he was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please just give me brief answers. I don't want to go into other details now. Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From June 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Jovan Maric?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Milan Gvero?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mico Grubor?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Petar Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I think he came during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Djordje Djukic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stevan Tomic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you about the commanders and the chiefs of staff of corps. Talic Momir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bosko Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grujo Boric?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mico Vlaisavljevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Novica Simic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Budimir Gavric?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was there from the beginning. I'm not sure though.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Radovan Grubac?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Vlado Spremo?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Radislav Krstic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He came a bit later, but he was there in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Milutin Skocajic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: From the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Zivomere Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bozo Novak?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me, when I say "yes," that means June, the month of June, when I was in the Main Staff and when I knew whether they were serving in the Army of Republika Srpska, that is, June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Bogdan Subotic, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Bogdan Subotic worked in the education centre in Banja Luka. After the Government of Republika Srpska was formed, he became the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Dusan Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He came later. At first he was with the Main Staff from the beginning, but when Bogdan Subotic was appointed advisor to the president of the republic for military issue, then Kovacevic took the position of minister of defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some numerical information about the level of staffing of the Main Staff and the status of these highest positions. Were all these highest positions filled in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon the adoption and the application of the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, but we had only so many officers that was sufficient to fill the basic positions because that created problems for us. I can't give you any percentage information; that would be pure guess-work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get new uniforms and new insignia once you became a member of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Immediately at the beginning, that is to say, in the summer of 1992, we didn't have new uniforms of the VRS, but in June we decided which insignia the VRS was going to wear. We had patches worn on our sleeves in the form of a tri-colour of Republika Srpska, and we had the same insignia on our caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do in order to improve the staffing of officers, the level of staffing of officers in the VRS at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: We immediately set up our personnel records of all the officers starting from sergeant to generals who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina or who had been sent for training from Bosnia-Herzegovina to other schools and education centres of the JNA. We believed that these officers, based on their place of birth and following the break-up of the SFRY, became citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it was their place to become commanding officers of one of the armies that was being formed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As we all know, at that time we had three armies of Bosnia-Herzegovina: The HVO which was made up of mostly Croats; then there was the B&H TO, Territorial Defence as they called themselves, which was the army of the Muslim people; and finally the Army of Republika Srpska made up of the majority of Serbs. But I have to note that, at the beginning, this last army had Croats and Muslims as well who were in favour of Yugoslav option. That was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that initially in the Army of Republika Srpska there were Croats and Muslims, are you referring to ordinary soldier or are you referring to officers or active-duty servicemen?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I know that there were professional officers of these ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the VRS was formed in the late 1991 and 1992, were there any cases of certain officers leaving the JNA and joining the armies above-mentioned?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: In 1991 when the war in Slovenia and Croatia started and later from April 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, professional officers of Croatian and Muslim ethnicities, both soldiers in war units of the JNA units deployed in those territories, and the officers left their units of their own volition and joined their respective ethnic armies. We in the personnel organs at the time after a certain period of time, I think it was five working days, decided that once somebody failed to report with their unit, we were obliged to institute proceedings to terminate their service in the JNA due to absence without leave. And such individual's service was terminated in the JNA because we knew that they had joined these newly formed armies in these new republics. Only a few or handful of officers, pro-Yugoslav oriented officers, remained in the JNA until its break-up. In early 1992, there were such officers in the Army of Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to those Croat and Muslim officers who were in the Army of Republika Srpska in the initial period?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: We, the officers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, thought that there won't be any major war, that everything would be over in a very short period of time. However, with the passage of time, we realised that this was not going to be the case, and these officers finally realised that it's not their place to be in the army that was fighting the Muslim and the Croatian armies. Some of them wanted to join the Yugoslav Army, the VJ, and some of them wanted to stay with the VRS until the very end. And I think these people, the latter group, came from mixed marriages. We didn't prevent them from remaining with the VRS. We first told them and gave approval to go on annual leave and then to be sent to the VJ. We just sent them on an annual leave to give them ample time to think it through. That was about for a month, and after that they would decide whether to join this new army and regulate the status. Because, at the time, the VJ was willing to accept these kind of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have document from 65 ter list of the Defence 003 -- sorry, yes, 0038D. 00038D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are going to see the English version shortly. This is a document issued by the Eastern Bosnian Corps and sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's dated the 25th of June, 1992. Mr. Malcic, can you tell us, are you familiar with this document, and what was the purpose of this document sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document. There were several documents of the same type at the beginning in June and July 1992. We acquired information in a variety of ways relating to the officers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina but who were serving in the Yugoslav Army. Some of them contacted us by telephone personally, expressing their wish to join the VRS, but they didn't know how. We put all this on paper. And through the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, we sent to the personnel administration of the VJ a request to allow these officers to join the VRS because there were quite a few of them. And we thought that everybody who was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina is entitled to join the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did these officers contact? What was the procedure in place at the time, and was the procedure altered subsequently?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Initially, these volunteers who wanted to come would go immediately to a corps command in their birth place, where they wanted to be, and where they thought they were most needed. Some of them contacted us in Han Pijesak as well. They declared themselves to be professional servicemen who wished to be assigned to wherever they are most needed by the VRS. However, there were those who, for various family reasons, didn't join the VRS. They rather decided to wait for providing for their family and then after that they would come and join the VRS because they thought they belonged there. After the withdrawal of the JNA in June from Bosnia-Herzegovina, many families were accommodated or placed in barracks as refugees. And even to this date, some of these families are still living in those VJ barracks which are not fit for living, because they didn't manage to solve their housing problems, and many of them are still living in rented flats in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who appointed them to serve in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: All the officers who subsequently joined the VRS were referred to, I think, under Article 271, to the Army of Republika Srpska. An officer in charge of the VRS would appoint all these officers according to war time and peacetime establishment adopted in June 1992 in compliance with the decree of the minister of defence that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were the criteria that this officer in charge applied? For example, if somebody came to Han Pijesak, what kind of criteria were applied for their appointment?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Once these officers came to Han Pijesak to the Main Staff, first we listened to their wishes, then we reviewed their education background, their rank, and we reviewed whether he was needed in his birth place. And, wherever it was possible, we would point them in the places where their families lived, of course depending on the rank and the need of the service. And once we have conducted these interviews, this kind of officer would say, Yes, I would accept this appointment. The main criterion was to send them to their birth place. That was the strongest point because they were willing to defend their families, their parents, and everybody else living in their birth place. And that is why they joined those units. There was a real danger of their families being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, we saw that throughout the war you were stationed at Han Pijesak, but we didn't discuss what happened to your family after the May events in 1992. Did your family go to Serbia or elsewhere? Can you just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think I said earlier that I had sent my daughters to Gacko. My wife later managed somehow with difficulties to leave Sarajevo and was reunited with our children. I found an appropriate accommodation for my family in Banja Luka where my father, mother, three brothers, and my other relatives lived there in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that your wife had tremendous difficulties in leaving Sarajevo. Do you know who prevented her from going out?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: After I was exchanged, when I reached Lukavica, I found out over the telephone - because there was a telephone that made it possible for us to contact persons in Sarajevo that was then under the command of the so-called TO army. My wife told me over the telephone that all the streets were blocked by armed persons who did not wear any kind of uniform or some of them had some black uniforms. They were breaking into apartments primarily of military personnel and mistreating families. Some groups came to our apartment where she was. They were armed with long rifles. They would fire a burst of gun-fire through the window and then they would say, Madam, where are your weapons? Or, Who was firing from your window? Who was firing at our soldiers? In one of these groups, there was a man who knew my wife. He knew her at the company where she had worked, and he said to her, You have to leave as soon as possible because you are a target of these groups of ours. I'm going to be with this group in this area only for another few days. If you don't leave, you are really going to be in bad trouble. A day or two later, a patrol that operated between my building and the building right next door was not on that road. Our assumption is that it was thanks to that man that they intentionally went elsewhere so that my wife would be able to leave that check-point, like another lady from the neighbourhood, and reach Serb territory. That was the last attempt to leave Sarajevo to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please relax a bit, Mr. Malcic. I just put this question, but I would now like to go back to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Your Honours, may I please tender this document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we admit it, I'd like to understand in the main heading it says Main Staff of the SR and then it's explained as Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Then the paragraph following at the end of it talks of officers are serving in the Army of the SR Yugoslavia. What does that mean? Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia? And what does that mean? FRY? Or what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the witness could deal with it, Your Honours. That would be the best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In June 1992, Republika Srpska was first called Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina rather. And later on it changed its name into Republika Srpska. That is why these terms overlap, as it were. The SRJ -- or, rather, the FRY was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was established consisting of Serbia and Montenegro, so that's that name. And before the break-up of Yugoslavia, the name was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which is the SFRY. So there is a lot of similarity involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness now explained the SR to us. In the English translation it says in parentheses "socialist republic," but it's not in B/C/S. It is actually an abbreviation for the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Muslims and Croats had just declared the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. Now, the SR Yugoslavia, is that the Serb Republic of Yugoslavia and what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, "Savezna Republika Jugoslavija."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Consisting of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D00212 [sic], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 292, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, since you worked in the personnel department, could you please give me a general answer so that the Trial Chamber and I could have a general picture. Out of the active-duty personnel who remained in the Army of Republika Srpska or who were later sent to the Army of Republika Srpska, their families, the majority of their families, did they have the same fate like your family? Did they remain in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? And if not, where did they go, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: After the war conflicts broke out, everyone sought shelter wherever they thought it would be best for their own family. Well, a "safe place," under quotation marks, if I can put it that way. Most of the families of the professional officers of the JNA went to the newly established Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and a smaller number even went to Macedonia because there were officers who married in those areas, so they went to stay with their in-laws, their families. A smaller part remained in the territory of Republika Srpska as was the case with my family and others who constituted a very small percentage, and they stayed for variety of reasons, family reasons, employment, and so on and so forth. A variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter [In English] 00188D.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see this on your screen, Mr. Malcic? Can you see this document?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the English back as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this is a call-up for service in the Army of Republika Srpska. Just a moment, please. Up here it says Obrenovic, Milomira Dragan, that is hand-written, and who signed this at the bottom in his own hand? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Underneath it says Mico Grubor?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: It says certified by, but it was signed by General Ratko Mladic in his own hand, and then it is certified by Colonel Mico Grubor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what this is now.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: We received information on the basis of a unit that had been founded in his place of birth, that there was a certain Captain Dragan Obrenovic who was there and who should come to join us. But the suggestion made was to send this call-up to him personally so that he could respond and come. We wrote this up. It was signed by the commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here that he should report to the command of Tactical Group Visegrad or directly to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska Han Pijesak barracks. Who was it that said that he should report to the Tactical Group of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: He was probably born in that area there, around Zvornik, Visegrad, I don't know exactly where, in that area. The Drina Corps had been established, and the Drina Corps was the one that ordered him to report to the Tactical Group Visegrad. Maybe he did report to us in Han Pijesak, but we deployed him in the Drina Corps where he wanted to go anyway because that's the territory where he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In which period during the course of the war, if we say that it started in May 1992 and went on until 1995, during which period of war did most of these officers come at this later date in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: The very beginning of the war, that is to say, in the summer of 1992 and the autumn of 1992, that's when most of the officers came because they felt it was necessary for them to join the Army of Republika Srpska. It was primarily at their own initiative. A smaller number had to be persuade to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document it admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D00293, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you a moment ago about the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have on our screens now document P191.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malcic, this is the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska that was passed on the 1st of June, 1992, as it says here. Were you aware of this law while you were in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
utterances.text: This is the basic document on the basis that we actually worked in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 1, can you see Article 1? Would you like it to be zoomed in a bit? We don't really have to read it. Could you just tell us who is it that the Army of Republika Srpska defends?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MALCIC
